editorial.headline: Health Support Services: Nationally Open, Bali Dependent on Scope
editorial.standfirst: This broad health-support activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but in Bali its PMA route turns on the precise service and risk level declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the less visible infrastructure that enables modern health care to function: blood-management units, medical and public-health laboratories, optometry providers, diagnostic centres and other medical-support services. Its scope also reaches specialised facilities, including stem-cell and cell-processing laboratories, eye and plasma banks, cell or tissue banks, biobanks, biorepositories, precision-medicine and genetic-testing facilities, hearing-aid centres, and optical services. It is a wide professional field, spanning both clinical support and the systems that preserve, analyse or make health-related material available.

The record places these services in the hands of operators managed by either government or private institutions. Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the activity is not one uniform operational model: a diagnostic centre, a genetic-analysis laboratory and a bank for biological material all sit within the same defined field, while performing distinctly different health-support functions. The registration choice must therefore follow the exact service being declared, rather than relying on the category’s broad title alone.

Nationally, the PMA position is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national signal, but it does not make the Bali position automatic. Bali’s status is scope-dependent: at the Besar scale, some included scopes are low risk while others carry a higher risk level. The provincial rule permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island. For this activity, PMA registration in Bali is available only when the applicant declares the higher-risk scope; the precise activity should be verified in live OSS.

The result is a category where the headline national openness is real, but not sufficient on its own for a Bali decision. A founder considering Bali must read the activity at service level: what is being operated, how it is classified for risk, and what is actually declared in OSS. The national ceiling remains 100%, while the local PMA route depends on that exact scope assessment.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not settle the Bali question: there, the precise health-support scope and its risk level decide whether PMA registration is available.
